papers.title_in_file: Solving nonlinear differential equations with differentiable quantum circuits
papers.version_note: File is arXiv v2 (18 May 2021); record title matches.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, numerical-example section (Fig. 6 discussion), Discussion and Conclusion. Methods and appendices skimmed by search only.
papers.what_it_is: A proposal and simulation of a hybrid quantum-classical algorithm in which differentiable quantum circuits (DQCs) built on quantum feature maps are trained to satisfy differential equations and boundary conditions.

assertions.value: The authors simulate their DQC algorithm on an instance of the Navier-Stokes equations and compute density, temperature and velocity profiles for fluid flow in a convergent-divergent nozzle; the simulation uses a full quantum state simulator in a noiseless setting.
assertions.anchor: Abstract, p. 1; Sec. on numerical example, p. 12
quotes: We simulate the algorithm to solve an instance of Navier-Stokes equations, and compute density, temperature and velocity profiles for the fluid flow in a convergent-divergent nozzle.
A full quantum state simulator is used in a noiseless setting.
assertions.certainty_reason: Numerical simulation of the authors' own algorithm on a noiseless simulator; no hardware.
assertions.reader_inference: The simulation is noiseless, so the result says nothing about performance on noisy devices.

assertions.value: In the paper's damped-oscillator test problem the product feature map fails to converge, the sparse Chebyshev map fails to converge at the harder setting, and the Chebyshev tower feature map continues to perform well; the authors state this supports the hypothesis that the feature map must be expressible enough for the problem.
quotes: The less powerful product feature map fails to converge with the loss quickly plateauing
The more expressible ChebT feature map continues to perform well
This supports the hypothesis that choosing a feature map expressible enough for the problem is important
assertions.certainty_reason: Measured on one test equation in noiseless simulation; the closing generalization is the authors' hypothesis.

assertions.value: The authors state they did not yet consider the impact of noise on the algorithm performance, and that they expect noisy black-box optimization and error mitigation to work with the method.
quotes: We did not yet consider the impact of noise on the algorithm performance
We expect recent developments in noisy black-box optimization algorithms for NISQ application would perform well in this method
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' own statement of scope; the expectation is unproven.

assertions.value: The authors discuss quantum advantage for differential equations as conditional: the success of operation depends on trainability of quantum circuits and on absolute operation rates, and trainability is known to suffer from barren plateaus.
quotes: the success of operation then depends on: 1) trainability of quantum circuits; 2) absolute operation rates.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' discussion, not a result; no advantage is demonstrated in the paper.

papers.title_in_file: Simulating a perceptron on a quantum computer
papers.version_note: File is arXiv v1 (11 Dec 2014); record title matches.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, quantum perceptron algorithm and complexity sections; later sections skimmed by search.
papers.what_it_is: A theoretical proposal of a quantum perceptron model, based on quantum phase estimation, that imitates the step-activation function of a classical perceptron.

assertions.value: The paper introduces a quantum perceptron model based on quantum phase estimation that imitates the step-activation function of a classical perceptron, and states it requires resources in O(n), where n is the size of the input.
quotes: this paper introduces a quantum perceptron model imitating the step-activation function of a classical perceptron. This scheme requires resources in O(n)
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' complexity statement for their own algorithm; analytic, with supporting simulation of precision.

assertions.value: The authors state that, for random inputs and weights, the precision of the algorithm has to increase with the number of neurons, and that their simulations indicate the required precision grows with n, which they describe as logarithmic growth.
quotes: The precision of the algorithm consequently has to increase with the number of neurons.
Of course, these considerations are only true for random input variables and parameters
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulation on random inputs only, as the authors themselves caveat.
assertions.reader_inference: The authors scope this to random inputs and parameters; realistic cases may differ.

assertions.value: The authors state that Altaisky's earlier quantum perceptron proposal has not been extended to a full neural network model, with the learning rule not preserving the unitarity of the weight operators.
quotes: Unfortunately, this proposal has not been extended to a full neural network model.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' characterization of prior work.

papers.title_in_file: Financial Fraud Detection using Quantum Graph Neural Networks
papers.version_note: File is arXiv v1 (3 Sep 2023); record title matches.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Secs. 4-7 (method, dataset, results, conclusion); related-work survey skimmed.
papers.what_it_is: An applied study that builds a quantum graph neural network with variational quantum circuits for credit card fraud detection and compares it with a classical GraphSAGE model on one public dataset.

assertions.value: The study uses the public credit card fraud dataset of European cardholders, which has only 492 frauds out of 284 807 transactions, and addresses the imbalance by random undersampling of non-fraud transactions.
quotes: The dataset is highly imbalanced, with only 492 frauds out of 284 807 transactions. To address this imbalance, we used random undersampling on the non-fraud transactions.
assertions.certainty_reason: Dataset description stated by the authors.

assertions.value: On this dataset the authors report QGNN accuracy of 94.5% against GraphSAGE accuracy of 92.3%, with the best QGNN configuration using 6 qubits and one layer.
quotes: Our experiments on a real-world financial dataset show that QGNNs can detect fraud with a remarkable accuracy of 94.5%, which is significantly higher than GNNs' accuracy of 92.3%.
assertions.certainty_reason: Single dataset, single reported run per configuration, no variance or significance test given in the sections read; undersampled data.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper gives no repeated runs or error bars in the sections read. The abstract's AUC 0.85 for the QGNN is a precision-recall AUC (Fig. 17) while the GraphSAGE AUC 0.77 is quoted from the ROC curve (Fig. 15), so the two AUC figures are not like for like. The file does not state hardware; quantum runs may be simulated.

assertions.value: The authors state the precision-recall AUC for the QGNN is estimated to be roughly 0.85, and they report that the GraphSAGE model achieves an AUC of 0.77.
quotes: The AUC for the precision-recall curve from Fig. 17 is estimated to be roughly 0.85
The GraphSAGE model achieves an AUC of 0.77, within the acceptable range for fraud classification tasks.
assertions.certainty_reason: Reported metrics from one experiment; metric types differ between the two models.

papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Sec. II.E.3 (Barren plateaus), Sec. IV (Conclusion and outlooks); other sections located by search only.
papers.what_it_is: A review of quantum classifiers: quantum support vector machines, kernel methods, decision trees, nearest neighbor, annealing classifiers and variational quantum classifiers, with barren plateaus, adversarial vulnerability and experiments.

assertions.value: The review states that McClean et al. showed that for a wide class of parameterized quantum circuits the probability that the gradient with respect to any variational parameter is exponentially suppressed as system size increases.
quotes: the probability that the gradient with respect to any variational parameters is exponentially suppressed as the system size increases.
assertions.certainty_reason: Review's description of a cited theorem.

assertions.value: The review states that, per its Ref. [140], if a global loss function is used barren plateaus typically appear even for circuits of small constant depth.
quotes: if a global loss function is used, then barren plateaus typically appear even for circuits with small constant depths.
assertions.certainty_reason: Review's description of a cited proof.

assertions.value: The review lists challenges to practical application: quantum random access memory is far from implementable at desirable scale, noise in quantum devices seems inevitable, and the question of a separation between variational classifiers and classical counterparts needs further study.
quotes: the quantum random access memory is a key component for a number of algorithms to demonstrate the potential advantages, while it is still far from implementing QRAM with a desirable scale at the current stage.
To find whether there is a separation between these models and their classical counterparts for potential future applications, further studies are highly desirable.
assertions.certainty_reason: Reviewers' assessment as of 2021.

assertions.value: The review states that Bittel and Kliesch proved the classical optimization problems for variational quantum algorithms are NP-hard, and that this presents a severe challenge for variational quantum classifiers.
quotes: Bittel and Kliesch proved that the classical optimization problems for variational quantum algorithms are
assertions.certainty_reason: Review's description of a cited proof; scope per the cited work.

papers.title_in_file: Theoretical Guarantees for Permutation-Equivariant Quantum Neural Networks
papers.version_note: File is arXiv v3 (14 Feb 2024); record title matches.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, main-text results (Theorems 1-3, trainability and generalization, numerics), Discussion; supplementary proofs located by search only.
papers.what_it_is: A theory paper that constructs Sn-equivariant quantum neural networks and proves trainability and generalization properties, with numerical checks on a graph-state classification task.

assertions.value: The authors state they prove that Sn-equivariant QNNs do not suffer from barren plateaus, quickly reach overparametrization, and generalize well from small amounts of data, and they verify with numerical simulations on a graph state classification task.
quotes: proving that they do not suffer from barren plateaus, quickly reach overparametrization, and generalize well from small amounts of data.
assertions.certainty_reason: Analytic proofs under stated assumptions (circuit depth forming independent 2-designs on isotypic blocks), plus simulations.

assertions.value: Theorem 3 states that an Sn-equivariant QNN can be overparametrized with a polynomial number of parameters.
quotes: Theorem 3 guarantees that Sn-equivariant QNNs only require a polynomial number of parameters to reach overparametrization.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated theorem.

assertions.value: The authors state their results were derived in the absence of noise, that noise would most likely weaken the trainability guarantees, and that absence-of-barren-plateau results in general leave datasets for which an otherwise trainable model is rendered untrainable.
assertions.anchor: Discussion, p. 10; Sec. on generalization, p. 8
quotes: while our results were derived in the absence of noise, it would be interesting to account for hardware imperfections.
Clearly, the presence of noise would change our analysis, and most likely weaken our trainability guarantees.
as there always exist datasets for which an otherwise trainable model can be rendered untrainable.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' explicit limitations.

papers.title_in_file: Bayesian Deep Learning on a Quantum Computer
papers.version_note: File is arXiv v3 (17 May 2019); record title matches the published 2019 version.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Background (Sec. II incl. quantum GP caveat), simulation and real-QPU sections, Conclusion; construction details in Sec. III skimmed.
papers.what_it_is: A quantum algorithm for Bayesian training of deep networks via their Gaussian-process connection, with noisy simulations and a restricted 2x2 matrix-inversion run on Rigetti and IBM devices.

assertions.value: The authors state that the quantum Gaussian process algorithm runs in logarithmic time only for sparse covariance matrices, which could restrict the form of the nonlinear function or other network parameters.
quotes: A caveat here is that the quantum algorithm only runs in logarithmic time for sparse covariance matrices
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' stated caveat on their algorithm's complexity.

assertions.value: The authors implemented a simplified, shallow-circuit version of the protocol on Rigetti's 8Q-Agave and IBM's IBMQX5 processors; the probability of protocol success on IBMQX5 is stated as 89%, translating to fidelity 0.78 with the expected state.
assertions.anchor: Sec. V (real QPU results), pp. 9-10, Fig. 3
quotes: we implement a simplified, shallow-circuit version of the protocol, and compare the outcome with the simulations
The probability of protocol success is 89%, which translates into a fidelity with the expected state of 0.78.
assertions.certainty_reason: Measured on real hardware, but only for a restricted 2x2 matrix inversion of about 20 gates.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper's own caveat is that the inverted matrix is small.

assertions.value: The authors state that their experimental results do not completely prove that the full protocol will be efficiently implementable on near-term quantum technologies.
quotes: these experimental results do not completely prove that the full protocol will be efficiently implementable in near-term quantum technologies.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' explicit limitation.

papers.title_in_file: Classical-to-quantum convolutional neural network transfer learning
papers.version_note: File is arXiv v2 (28 Sep 2023), the revised version; record year 2023 is consistent, filename carries 2022 (v1).
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Sec. 4 (Simulation results), Sec. 5 (Conclusion); Sec. 2-3 and appendices skimmed by search.
papers.what_it_is: A numerical study of transfer learning in which a pre-trained classical CNN feeds a quantum convolutional neural network, benchmarked on MNIST binary classification tasks with PennyLane simulation.

assertions.value: The simulations use PennyLane on MNIST binary tasks (0 vs. 1, 2 vs. 3, 8 vs. 9) with a classical CNN pre-trained on 60,000 Fashion-MNIST data; the QCNN has eight input qubits loading 256 features by amplitude encoding and is fine-tuned on 10,000 MNIST samples.
quotes: All C2Q-CNN simulations were performed with eight input qubits, to which the amplitude encoding loads 256 features.
These output values are then encoded into 8 input qubits of the QCNN, which is fine-tuned using 10,000 MNIST data samples.
assertions.certainty_reason: Experimental setup as reported by the authors.

assertions.value: In these simulations the C2Q models consistently reached higher classification accuracy than the classical-to-classical transfer models, with fewer trainable parameters; a Welch's t-test indicated statistically significant advantage for selected ansatzes.
quotes: the C2Q models consistently achieved higher classification accuracy compared to the C2C models, despite having fewer trainable parameters.
have a statistically significant quantum advantage over both 1D and 2D classical models for all classification problems
assertions.certainty_reason: Noiseless classical simulation on three MNIST binary tasks, results averaged over ten random initializations; advantage holds for some ansatzes, not all.
assertions.reader_inference: Per the paper, C2Q was not higher for ZX pooling with convolution 1 and 3 in the 2 vs. 3 task. Tasks are easy binary subsets of MNIST.

assertions.value: The authors state that the reason behind the quantum advantage demonstrated by C2Q-CNN remains unclear, that rigorous analysis is lacking, and that whether it holds with more trainable parameters and other datasets is open.
quotes: First, the reason behind the quantum advantage demonstrated by C2Q-CNN remains unclear.
verifying whether the quantum advantage would continue to hold as the number of trainable parameters increases and for other datasets would be interesting.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' explicit limitation.
